[h3] Thanks, Capcom. [/h3]
I haven't enjoyed playing games this much in a long time, but RE4 brought back long forgotten feelings and emotions. Definitely the best Resident Evil remake of all three so far.
What happens when you remake the greatest game ever? You get the greatest game ever, again.

Some games are ones you delete after you finish them.

Some games are ones you remember even years later.

Resident Evil 4 falls into the second category for me.

When I first started playing, I thought I was just going to play a high-quality remake. But as the hours passed, I realized that Capcom hadn't just revamped an old game; they had brought back to life a legend that players have loved for years.

The atmosphere is incredible. From the moment you enter the village, you constantly feel pressure. You don't know what's around the next corner, you're not sure if you have enough ammunition, and you always feel like something is going to go wrong. That's what makes Resident Evil 4 special.

Leon is fantastic as always. His more mature and experienced self adds a new depth to the story. The side characters, boss battles, and unforgettable scenes have also been meticulously recreated.

The gameplay is addictively good. You think, "Let me play one more level," then you look at the clock and it's midnight. The combat is fluid, inventory management is still fun, and the knife mechanics add a whole new flavor to the game.

But what impressed me most was this:

This game reminded me why I love video games.

It gave me an experience where I didn't have to constantly follow quest markers, waste time on unnecessary things in an open world, and was simply immersed in a well-designed adventure.

Many games today strive to offer larger maps, more content, and longer gameplay.

Resident Evil 4, however, chooses to simply be fun.

And it does it almost perfectly.

If you've played this game before, it will remind you why it's a classic.

If you're playing it for the first time, you'll understand why everyone has been talking about Resident Evil 4 for years.

Some games are the best of their time.

Some transcend their time.

Resident Evil 4 is one of them.

[h1]18 years later, still a Masterpiece![/h1]

After RE3 Remake, when Capcom announced that they were doing a remake for RE4, I was so happy; but at the same time, was scared that it would follow the path of RE3.
But believe me, while playing this masterpiece you won't think of RE3 anymore, and in my opinion, it was close enough to what we needed.

From the start, you'll notice that some places are changed and almost unrecognizable, but after playing for a few minutes, that old RE 4 shows itself within this game, but with almost real-life graphics!

here we have Capcom making you ready for the changes that you'll see further into the game. while showing you that they tried their best to be faithful. surely that has its ups and downs, but I can live with that.

[h1]The Gameplay[/h1] is almost perfect; at first, I was worried that enemies were unreliable on being stunned when you shoot them in the face since sometimes it takes more than two hits for them to get stunned. But at the end of the game, there I was, blasting through them like a bunch of predictable insects. Sure, Leon's walking is a little heavy, but it doesn't make it any less fluid.
The map is fantastic, this was the first Resident Evil game in that I used its map more than 100+ times in one playthrough, and I was using it for gathering treasures and doing requests for HOURS!

Gunplay was great for me with all of the guns except with TMP, that gun will never shoot where you tell it to shoot, and I only used it 2 or 3 times when I was out of ammo on other guns, or I was trying to kill some nasty dogs with Nemesis-like teeth.

[h1]The story[/h1] was expended much more, and there was so much to find out about the plaga and Los Iluminados, the Salazar family, and the betrayal of Ramon. 
also finding out why Ada wants the sample or why Wesker needs it.
We get more information about Major Krauser and his operation with Leon. and even get to know more about our Madridan officer Louis Sera.
I think they're changing the whole story of Operation Javier, but it doesn't sound bad though.

[h1]Graphics[/h1] are at the peak! I'm not sure if ReEngine can make it further in this matter from here on forward; the lighting is so cool, and you'll appreciate that when playing as Ashley.
There were some rainy moments in a section of the village that made my fps cry in its bed, but I can't call that non-optimized, because It was so beautiful and I was playing on Ultra 4K so I expected some fps drops.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2953192782

[h1]Ashley[/h1]is GREAT Now! She's no more a loud screaming machine that can't even climb down a ladder, but instead, you'll be amazed by the amount of help that she provides to Leon; I started to like her from the church encounter, there is more soul put into her and that was the best change they've made in the remake.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2951472683

[h1]Cons[/h1]
Some boss fights were changed a lot and even built new from the ground up, like [spoiler]Salazar[/spoiler] and I didn't like that.
Fight with Krauser wasn't like old times and the area felt so empty; they even changed [spoiler] Krauser's mutated hand[/spoiler] and it was much uglier than the original.

Some areas were a little bit smaller than the original, which was odd.

Merchant's voice was a downside; it felt like he was trying to mimic or even mock the original voice actor; I don't exactly know why, but It felt like I was talking to the duke from ReVillage. But Then I remembered that Duke didn't talk this much; even if he did, I didn't care.
But the merchant...ooh boy, he is so talkative now, Shut up already! I am trying to choose something to buy, don't give me that repetitive dialogue every second; 
and his dialogue doesn't always mean something; for example, he sometimes says he got some rare things on sale but I the stranger couldn't find anything in his pockets.
Speaking of pockets, the only good and funny thing he said was that I couldn't put that Rocket launcher in my pocket.

[h1]Overall[/h1] the game feels so much like the old RE4, and in some cases even better; the action is like John Wick killing a bunch of farmers, but at some points, the Horror is Unbearable! w8 until you encounter and try to defeat the first two Regeneradors while looking for that Biosensor Scope.

The BIG undeniable flaw of RE4 Remake, which cannot be completely ignored, is simplifying or removing several challenging situations that were present or more engaging in the original version, especially from the island.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Some video games are so good, that everyone should experience them at least once. When Resident Evil 4 was released in 2005, it was considered as such. The remake of Resident Evil 4 is a good reminder of this fact too.
Experience this Masterpiece at all costs!

I played through the original from 2005 about 7 times on the highest difficulty level.

The new title is called a remake, but many areas have been changed and familiar bosses and enemies have been used in other places, you can like that, but you don't have to. There are also one or two new settings, so some things are new and make you want to play through, that's how it should be.

The graphics and atmosphere are really very well done, in my opinion the best part of the whole series. The light and shadow effects are really impressive. The new missions like medallion shooting are also fun, which was great in the original.

The game itself has become harder, in some places it has a bit of a Dark Souls feel, because you just die without warning or enemies that used to come slowly (Regenerador) now come crawling and jump at you, the traps are also much better laid and the game sometimes turns into work. You are also no longer invincible when you perform combat animations, many enemies no longer stop when you shoot at them and absorb many shots like a sponge. Killing enemies from behind without being noticed is a nice feature.

You can no longer kick doors in either and ammunition (if you get it) is used up again straight away because the areas are just packed with enemies, it sometimes feels like Killing Floor. You are constantly crafting ammunition and shooting.

To be completely honest, when it comes to graphics, sound and atmosphere then it is definitely Resident Evil 4 Remake, but when it comes to authentic areas, nice speed runs or relaxed gaming then definitely the original. I see the remake more as a parallel game to the original. I like them both.

Now for the negative point, what I didn't like so much: In the original, the Separate Ways expansion was included for free, in the remake you have to shell out extra money for it, and 2 weapons or costumes that aren't available in the game can only be obtained via microtransactions, so here again they want to really cash in and milk the player. Keyword: Fear of missing out (FOMO). And then there are special suitcases or talismans that make the game easier because you get more resources, money or buy special upgrades. Microtransactions in a single-player game? I think that's really stupid.

I only got the main game + Separate Ways and it was worth it.

I completed this new game version on PS5 and now on PC, and I'm generally pleased with the revisions. In my opinion, the PC version is better than consoles. Some of the changes are extremely severe, such as when particular people die or how they are presented, and they alter the tone and impact of the plot. However, I agree that they stuck true to the original to a large extent, and they tried their best to keep the game appealing, enjoyable, and full of personality. I liked what they did with Ashley; in the original, she was annoying and seemed helpless, like a large burden who shrieked frequently, but her remake version appears more authentic, and her connection with Leon appears more natural as it develops throughout the game, with their confidence in each other growing stronger. 

Ashley is a fun companion in this game, and I believe she brings a lot of personality to the game, some of which was not even present in the original. The NG+ and professional prizes are good and give some incentive to retry the game. The combat is really incredible. Each scenario now has additional depth and player options. The counterattack system is fun to learn, and the ability to hide mechanics gives you even more ways to approach each combat. The gun noises are flawless, the new gore system is vicious, and the enemy AI is significantly more terrifying and hostile. The knife is also more intuitive and streamlined, allowing you to slash without initially equipping or stab when equipped. The finishers are also fantastic, reducing the need to swip each downed adversary like a fool. 

When you combine this with freshly added ragdoll physics, destructible environments, new weapons, charms, and an infinite knife, the replay value skyrockets. Also, knife durability is important for balancing and making decisions. The tale and characters are more developed and fleshed out than in the original. Leon has a slightly more dramatic history, but he retains his charisma, charm, and sense of humor. Luis is given significantly more screen time and speech than before, allowing him to form a bond with Leon and have a true character/redemption arc. They even added files to his narrative and history with Umbrella. Krauser has also significantly improved. His past with Leon is substantially explored in the remake, adding to the emotional stakes and sense of betrayal that Leon is feeling. Moreover, Ashley is also far more solid, capable, and relatable than she was previously. 

Her relationship with Leon developed more organically and convincingly throughout the game, and I felt like she had earned a lot of confidence and experience by the end. Many people are complaining about Ada, but I believe they are exaggerating. Each individual's own. It was fantastic to see some of the Separate Ways storylines included in the main campaign. The remake also includes a lot of mythology that focuses on the game's religious and occult elements. From my perspective, the game is frightening. The increased distinction between light and dark is a wonderful improvement. 

To conclude, the enhanced lighting and gorgeous skyboxes add to the gothic/folkloric ambiance and make opponents appear considerably creepier when they appear from around corners or behind you. The terror has been substantially intensified, and the plagas are more horrific and can even grab onto enemies. New enemy varieties, such as the brutal and "broken neck" Ganados, are extremely aggressive and entertaining to combat. Conclusion, I hope that in the next remake, Resident Evil 5 Remake, they can give Albert Wesker a new ending and continuing using his personality because Resident Evil is about Albert Wesker.

Final Score: 9.5

I didn’t go into Resident Evil 4 expecting much. I’m not really a hardcore fan of the series, and survival horror isn’t usually my main thing. But somehow, this game completely pulled me in mostly because of its story.

At first, it feels like a simple mission: Leon S. Kennedy is sent to rescue the president’s daughter. Nothing too special on paper. But as the game progresses, it turns into something much deeper and more intense. The atmosphere, the mysterious village, and the strange cult all build a really strong sense of tension. I found myself wanting to keep playing just to see what would happen next.

Leon as a character is surprisingly enjoyable. He’s calm, confident, and sometimes even a bit sarcastic, which makes the dialogue feel natural instead of forced. The interactions between characters don’t feel overly dramatic they feel human, and that made the story more engaging for me.

What really stood out was how the game balances action and horror. It’s not just about being scared — it’s about being constantly on edge. You’re never fully comfortable, and that keeps the experience exciting. Even though I’m not a big fan of horror games, I didn’t feel overwhelmed. Instead, I felt curious and invested.

The pacing is also very well done. The game keeps introducing new elements without making things feel repetitive. Just when you think you’ve seen everything, something new shows up and changes the situation.

Overall, Resident Evil 4 made me interested in the series in a way I didn’t expect. It’s not just a good game it’s a game that can turn someone who isn’t even a fan into someone who wants to explore more. If the rest of the series offers even half of what this game delivers in terms of story and atmosphere, then I’m definitely in.

Resident Evil 4 offers the most fledged out and longest experience yet (Out of the remakes.) It is a massive improvement in nearly every area. The graphics make a slight jump and the UI, map size and gameplay mechanics receive a nice polish on top of other major improvements.

RE4R plays out much more like a spy movie in a sense. Being sent to save the presidents daughter is quite a daunting task, but to do it alone? A whole other level. Leon now being a weathered vet of the Raccoon City incident is back in the action and his main character syndrome is now much more pronounced with his even cheesier one liners and enhanced combat. 

This is a big jump in terms of combat from the other remakes. With the leap from 3 to 4 being much larger than the leap from 2 to 3. There is now a parry system for certain attacks and the guns feel better than RE3R. The case function is a fantastic addition that I thought was really neat and it only got better the longer I got through the story. Adding the charms to the cases and the shooting range was a really neat side task that gave me some reprieve in between chapters. 

The writing was fantastic as well. When I said it was playing out like a spy movie, I meant it. The dialogue, the comms communications with [spoiler]Roost and Ada/others[/spoiler], the chase of common interests between multitudes of characters and the "race against the clock" kind of feeling was well induced because the game makes you [b][u]CARE[/u][/b] about the characters. 

Speaking of the characters, I found that this game had the strongest cast of characters so far. Mainly because it was able to introduce and expand upon some of these characters stories and motivations throughout the length of the entire game, allowing for them to complete arcs and development. Ashley was adorable and truly grew by the end of the game. Luis was fantastic and had his own little arc throughout the story. [spoiler]From a character that I thought would be killed off early to managing to make it through 2/3's of the game was quite a neat switch up. [/spoiler] Roost was present and I wish we got a bit more of involvement with her, however it would've been quite hard to implement into the storyline. 

Just like in RE3R compared to RE2R there is definitely much more action than horror in this game. Which in Resident 3's remake I thought was a net negative as the rest of that game felt unsure in what it wanted to be. However for RE4R, I find that the more action based storytelling and gameplay is well intertwined with more tense and suspenseful moments (And the fact that the game is significantly longer than 3's remake helps) such as playing as [spoiler]Ashley in the library and having to go weaponless for a period of time in order to reunite with Leon. Making your past all of the dead down in the pit full of spikes and turning back on the power. Powering up the doors and leveling up the keycards while dealing with the Regeneradors.[/spoiler] Moments like that brought me back to the feelings I got when I was first playing RE2R for the first time. [spoiler](Something that RE3R missed entirely because I thought Jill and Carlos were both combat-wise very capable and didn't offer too much of a changeup in gameplay when we swapped as them.) [/spoiler]

There is a lot to explore and scavenge around and unlike in RE3R, I felt like I could genuinely explore and take in the breathtaking setting that the game finds itself in. All of the different settings this game covers is quite impressive, from the decrepit villages that are amuck with ruin, the vastness of the castles with tight corners and grand decor, to the mines - the game has plenty of backdrops and environments that all offer a different feel to the experience. It truly makes it feel like a journey throughout the whole ordeal. Nothing gets too stale or overdone and while some of the sections feel quite over the top - [spoiler]The mine section on the rail cart with Luis! Which also, was quite a loss for the ladies of the world.[/spoiler] everything feels quite in line for Resident Evil :)

Something that I noticed gameplay wise was that I wasn't in dire need of ammo as often as the other games. Mainly because of the new melee system allowing me to manage to save a bit more ammo than normal. It helped that the game had plenty of resources and the merchant to aid in ammo acquisition. At times it felt like I almost had [i]too[/i] much ammo, but it would be depleted quickly and didn't feel too unbalanced. 

The length of the game was something that I was not expecting. It was a welcome change from the 6-10 hour campaigns that the 2 and 3 remakes offered. However there was times where it sort of felt a bit drawn out, particularly towards the end of the game. Thankfully the game is entertaining enough and it wrapped up a few of the loose ends to help tie the ending of the game together well. The main story once completed offers more ways to enjoy the game than just replaying the story. The mercenaries mode and Separate Ways modes/stories are also awaiting once finished, which is really neat and will definitely have me coming back to play again.

As with my previous reviews for the modern RE remakes, I wholeheartedly recommend this game to the casual/newcomer and hardcore RE fans. It offers an experience that, so far, is not rivaled by the other RE games that I have played. It knows what it is and plays into it wholly and for that I think it is vying for my favorite RE experience so far. It definitely feels like the developers were able to take their time with this remake and were able to [i]mostly[/i] keep it faithful to the original while still making improvements that elevated the game. 

Time for a little RE hiatus :)

Resident Evil 4 is really really good and probably the best resident evil game out there right now at least in gameplay. 

Capcom basically took everything that worked so well in Resident Evil 2 & 7, dialed up the action and gameplay by 10 while still managing to keep the iconic horror this franchise is known for. They have successfully struck the perfect balance between action packed power fantasy gameplay, and  iconic resident evil horror. This is something most studios can't achieve, yet Capcom not only did it, but also perfected it in this game.

The cut scenes, the environments, the art direction, the carefully designed details on every surface, it's all done with such surgical perfection and it's only further enhanced by the buttery smooth optimisation of this game. No stutters, No frame rate drops, not even a single bug to encountered in my entire 30 hour playthrough. Every section, level, terrain, item and location not only looks gorgeous, but plays perfectly and just like how it's supposed to. I cannot commend the people behind this engine and games enough. Truly talented tech geniuses and its their innovation that set the ground work for what has made this franchise ascend into god tier quality.

What makes this game stand out so much though is the gameplay. Third-person Blood-curdling action packed linear levels with satisfying gun play that is only further enhanced by Capcom's insane sound design. Every foot step, every gun shot, even something as small as the sound of pages turning is so detailed. When you shoot someone in the head, you feel the impact of the bullet from the sound of skin tearing and blood splatter. When you round house kick, you feel the heavy impact of leon's foot on the enemies neck from the sound of it snapping and cracking. It really brings this game to life. It is truly a technical marvel and i swear no one in this industry does sound as good as capcom does.

Its all further enhanced by the variety of weapons & upgrades in this game. There's enough here to keep a healthy level of flexibility in how you want to play. The progression system in how you upgrade your weapons is also incorporated into exploration, making it always feel rewarding and worth while. The enemies follow suit in quality, ranging from your classic terrifying big monster with dodge mechanics to a slippery assassin scorpion that intelligently uses the environment to sneak up and attack you. Many also have little twists and details that really enrich the way you can approach enemies. Villagers that hold C4's in their hand that you can shoot to blow them and their surroundings up. Infected with regenerative abilities that you need to shoot specific weak spots to kill. It's this rich variety in how you interact with the game that makes the moment to moment experience always feel new. It is what makes this franchise so iconically endlessly replayable.

The story is about what you'd expect from a capcom resident evil game. Nothing insane in narrative, but just enough lore dressing and interesting connections to umbrella to keep fans like me interested in the characters of this game and the world their in. What surprised me the most though is how hilarious the writing is. Leons dialogue in particular. It's bordering Devil may cry 5 levels of ironic but still being grounded enough to feel serious. I think the execution is the real MVP here as it's done well enough to make Leon's silly 2010 esq comments come off as charming and lovable rather than cringe and annoying. The writing really is a product of its time and i'm so happy Capcom did not touch it in this remake because i really love it.

Generally speaking, this extreme of a departure in any franchise, let alone one with horror as iconic as Resident Evil's, usually turns out to be a disappointment. But Capcom really stuck the landing here. They managed to create a satisfying action focused game whilst still having it feel like resident evil. They did it so well, infact, i might prefer this style over RE 2&7's more slow placed horror, as long as it's done well. 

And this game certainly does it extremely well. Which is why I highly recommend it.

Resident Evil 4 is the latest series of remakes produced by Capcom after the releases of Resident Evil 2 and 3 in 2019 and 2020 respectively. After the previous, albeit they were quite short, sensational creations, I didn't expect Resident Evil 4 to be any different compared to its predecessors at all. The experience was totally different from the ones of RE 2 and 3, which played on certains parts of the devastated city of Racoon. You are thrown into a rural area controlled by insane, vicious and mercyless cultists seeking to take over the entire planet. The gameplay is faster and much more action-oriented compared to the two previous games. It hardly ever felt like even a single minute was wasted with just sneaking around and stumbling across nothing. That means the whole 15-20 hours of gameplay are fully utilized.

Enemies move in a dangerous, erractic manner and having them overwhelm and surrounding you happens so quickly that you can never really feel safe, so making snap decisions when it comes to prioritising targets is extremely important. You also have to be aware of the surface you're walking on, as it's not uncommon to get your foot stuck in a bear traps, which can turn out to be very problematic, especially during a fight. You might have a very expansive tollset, but that doesn't mean you can afford to lose focus or be unaware of your surroundings.
A one-size fits all strategy doesn't work in this game, as the enemies can suddenly pull up with shields or helmets forcing you to use different styles how to exterminate the hostile targets.

What starts as a very straightforward rescue mission, with Leon Kennedy being tasked to locate and free the US President's missing daughter, Ashley, soon turns into a heart-stopping series of bloody clashes against giant sea monsters, crazed hordes in boarded up cabins and bloodythirstly, possesed cultists in and around a heavily fortified castle, skulking sections through shadowy laboratories, explosive and thrilling minecart chases and countless run-ins with some twisted and insane freaks infected with the dangerous Las Plagas parasite.

Additionally it's noteworthy to mention how terrifying and frightening the audio design is. When it comes to a cultivating sense of dread, that game almost belongs to the "unreachable" category. Whether it's the manic chanting of the parasite-mutated peasant farmers or the snarl of wolvees as they wander through the area around you in the castle's confusing hedge maze. All of which had me at the edge of my seat, you can believe that.

When you need to take a breather in order to restack your ammo, heal up, get recipes to craft exact desired ammo types, increase the capacity of your case or simply purchase new weapons, a mysterious merchant always having a saying ready, returns to give Leon the chance to get fully equipped before moving on to the next chapter. Furthermore, you can complete certain tasks (e.g. shooting down hidden blue medallions, killing a small amount of rats in certain, small areas, tracking down a rare golden chicken egg) written down on flyers distributed across the whole map in exchange for spinel gemstones which can be traded for unique items and upgrades.

The question whether to give this game a shot or not is a total no-brainer. It's just the perfect fit for action-horror fans. The  world is just so beautifully designed with lots of surprises, fun, plently of explorable areas and tasks to be completed. To be honest, I didn't particuarly like this game at the beginning, because I'm not the biggest fan of this cult, medieval-like stuff and clearly prefer the atmosphere, world and vibe of the Resident Evil 2 and 3 games. The design of the inventory is also something I didn't particular like and I clearly preferred the one from RE 2 and 3 as well. Moreover, the different mixtures of yellow, red and green herbes was way to confusing. However, this game finally started to grow on me during chapter 11, from which I had an intense 3.5 hour stint till the end of chapter 13. From then on I was glad to not have given up on that masterpiece to early.

Rarely could a remake/rewrite achieve the levels Resident Evil 4 reached. Now that it's been a few years since this release, I have the thoughts to write my review.

Vastly different in tone from the original, there was a bar set so high that an Olympic pole-vaulter easily could've missed, and yet they managed to craft a refreshing experience on the foundation of the bones, marrow and chilled blood of the RE4 we all know and love.

RE4 is arguably my favorite video game of all time, I played through it more times than I could count since I was young and loved it equally or more every time. This remake satisfied essentially every itch to be scratched, the greatly improved script (I love the campiness of the original, but a 1:1 remake would've been eye-rolling), smooth controls that lend themselves to the action-oriented terror and that ever-familiar atmosphere throughout the very extensive journey of our leading man Leon Kennedy. 

One of the most impactful changes they made was the rewrite of Ashley's character. I didn't have too many issues with the original, but in RE4R, she is so very well fleshed out and charming, contributing a depth and investment in her dynamic with Leon and the violent, horrifying world closing in around them. Not to mention her cheering you on in the shooting gallery was just about the most motivating thing possible. Excellent voice acting and character progression, I give an earnest thank-you to the writers for giving us this new look at a character we spend a great deal of time with.

The lore presented through collectibles gives us much more insight into the characters as well, and while optional, I'm always glad when developers provide us with snippets into the thoughts, emotions and lives of those who inhabit the world we are plugged into. More than once I was caught off guard by how moved I was by the backstories of certain characters, and that connection only deepened my experience with the game as whole.

The challenge still exists, I went with the confidence of a veteran RE4 player on the higher difficulties and found myself more than adequately impressed with how often I found myself on the back foot. The enemies don't just feel like fodder. The bosses are not only imposing, but quite cinematic in the same vein as the original.

There's a true sense of accomplishment when you reach the end of this journey, and I couldn't be happier with what they changed, what they maintained, and what they greatly improved. As with the original, the replay value is vast.

It's okay to be afraid...and it's also okay to stick a knife in the neck of a bloodthirsty Los Plagas trying to cut your head off. All that matters is you keep moving forward.

This remake will probably hold the crown of being the best remake I’ve ever played for a very long time. It’s the quintessential definition of the word “remake” and how it should be made.

I already reviewed Resident Evil 4 (2005), where I’ve pointed out the very core aspects of the series, genre, and such. But the remake version of RE4 deserves every little bit of attention it gets, and this review is not an exception.

Starting off with the very basics: it is still a survival horror game, with the elements of action. Lots of elements of action.

Is the game still a horror comedy? Nope, CAPCOM decided to keep the newly created tone of narration, continuing the journey of the legendary Leon Scott Kennedy from RE2 Remake.
Instead of the corny joke-cracking, one-liner-spitting, kickass special agent Leon, we now have a more morally grounded version of him. He is traumatized by the events of previous RE installments and acts way more serious than in the original version of the game.

Does that make him a boring character? Not by a long shot: instead, he now has his own charm, not to mention his physique and face model, which earned him the title of being the most handsome male character that has ever existed in the gaming industry, by the opinion of the major part of gamers themselves.

Story-wise we got some retcons: something changed here, some areas were replaced completely with classical ones being cut there, Los Illuminados’ ambitions are much more serious instead of following the typical trope of “being cartoonishly evil and wanting to rule the world because of power and wealth,” a more fleshed-out Separate Ways campaign, and so on.
Were all the changes good? That’s a point of debate for many in the RE4 community.

Someone mentions the retconned personalities of Lord Saddler and Ramon Salazar: instead of being present as much as in the previous game, they tend to appear less frequently, and their personalities become way too boring and cliché for some, but on the other hand, developers added a lot of clues that point to their background history, making them feel more complex.

Someone mentions Luis Serra: someone likes his corny charm from the original version of the game, and someone likes the Don Quixote version of him from the remake.

Someone mentions the areas that got reconstructed and reimagined. Now, for example, instead of being able to choose the way we go in the Village (between the Subway Surfers game with a giant or going for a tea with the chainsaw-wielding Bella Sisters), it is now linear: we are bound to meet the Bella Sisters.
All in all, all of the aforementioned changes are debatable, but we’ll get to that later.

Gameplay-wise there were quite a lot of changes too: QTEs were removed completely (which for me is not a very good thing, because it added some aspect of pacing to the story), head-scratching puzzles became way too simple, we’ve got a parry mechanic with the need of repairing and upgrading our beloved knife, we got stripped of incendiary grenades, getting a heavy grenade instead, and so on and on. Spinels now serve a purpose instead of being a 2000-peseta pickup, and the merchant now has much more complex mechanics in general.

The attention to detail is astonishing: most of the ways you could have cheesed your fights in the original game got nerfed (hello there Village Tower), the game’s audio has perfect design in a way that the sounds of crafting ammo or parrying an attack buzz your ears in a very specific, comfy way, and the sound of a chainsaw or your knife breaking will put you in panic mode almost instantly. The sound of death sounds heavy but not that over-the-top, which makes you want to accept your momentary defeat and continue on your way in trying to complete a certain area.
The guns feel like… guns, with the respective sound and level of recoil, and I can talk about such things for a very long time, but it is already a love letter to the game that I’m writing rather than just a simple, stalled-out review.

The soundtrack is awesome too: it partly consists of the original game’s OST remixes, which was truly a blessing to hear once again in a remake after almost 20 years.

The graphical aspect of the game is very… let’s say, balanced. There isn’t much to render; the locations are pretty small and straightforward, but that’s exactly what allowed the developers to focus on improving the quality of the game’s looks in certain areas. For example, Village’s color filter changes depending on the time of day, and if the game happens to think that you have to experience a very dark and hollow corridor, the lighting goes away in a very gentle, unnoticeable manner.

The optimization is also great: on the 4060 you can squeeze 100+ FPS playing with the Ultra settings. The game supports the expansion of VRAM with the cost of the regular RAM, it has FSR3 implemented (which blurs the graphics a bit too much for my liking, but it’s still there), and overall, it didn’t crash nor freeze on me even once.

The negative sides of the game are mainly the oversimplification of the puzzles and the removal of some things that were standing out in the original.
All of the puzzles have hints in, say, letters, which are colored green, and every interactable object was brashly painted with yellow, for some reason.
Picture this: you walk amongst the centuries-old castle, maintained by the aristocratic family of Salazars, which has zombies as their security, but for some reason there are a ton of yellow-painted boxes and barrels, and for some reason even bird’s nests, ladders, windows, and doors are yellow. And it all makes you question - “why?”. It is a way to make the game more accessible for gamers, but the way it was implemented sure is questionable.

Or take incendiary grenades as a previously mentioned example. There wasn’t much use for them in the original game anyway, and instead of creating a need for them, developers decided to replace them with ever-so-conveniently placed fire barrels or, to bring a more specific example, fire lamps, which swing left and right with no reason in particular, making a very screeching noise, which basically says, “heyyy, I’m hanging there; shoot me. I can deal damage.”

I should also mention the “adaptive difficulty” mechanic. For some reason this exact mechanic seems to be one of the most beloved at CAPCOM: if you play well, the game becomes harder; if you play badly, the game becomes easier.
What exactly is the point in letting the player choose the level of difficulty if the game has aspects of scaling changed without the player’s permission anyway? You can read about that on the Internet; there are quite a lot of sources confirming the implementation of such a mechanic.

We also stripped off some running gags or jokes, which by today’s standards would sound unacceptable for most. Is it good or bad? That’s completely up to you.

Overall—I love this game. It easily is one of my favorites, being somewhere along the top 3 best video games I’ve ever played. I adore everything about Resident Evil 4: the gameplay is incredibly addictive, the replayability value is unimaginable, and you can get lost in this game for hundreds of hours easily. Leon Kennedy is one of my favorite characters, and I am looking forward to seeing how his story is going to continue in Requiem, and, maybe, who knows, someday Ashley Graham will make an appearance, which would be great.

Regarding the debate that the remake changes created? There, let me provide a solution for you: play both versions of the game! That way you’ll earn the complete experience of Resident Evil 4: a game that every single gamer out there should complete in one way or another, and that way you’ll decide what you like more in each of the versions.

Fantastic remake, improving an already great game in almost every way.

Graphics are amazing. The character models are incredibly detailed, the enemies look disgusting and terrifying, and the environments are gorgeous. The village, castle, and island all look fantastic, with much more detail, atmosphere, and environmental storytelling than the original. The lighting is especially good, making dark areas feel genuinely threatening. The animations are also excellent, with much more realistic character movement, enemy reactions, and combat animations. Everything feels modern and polished while still retaining the identity of the original game.

Sound effects are fantastic. The weapons sound powerful, the enemies sound terrifying, and the environmental sounds do a great job of creating tension. Hearing Ganados talking, shouting, and communicating with each other makes encounters feel chaotic and unpredictable. The music is also great, and the more atmospheric approach works really well during exploration. The voice acting is excellent, with much more natural performances than the original game. Some of the cheesy dialogue is still there, but thankfully most of it feels much more natural this time around.

Gameplay is great and very engaging. The combat from the original has been greatly improved, with much more responsive movement and a lot more options during encounters. Leon can now move while aiming, crouch, parry attacks with his knife, and perform stealth takedowns. These additions make combat much more fluid and give you more ways to approach every situation. You can play aggressively, carefully pick enemies off from a distance, or use stealth to avoid unnecessary fights.

The inventory system remains excellent. The attaché case is still one of the most satisfying inventory systems in gaming, letting you organize your weapons, ammunition, healing items, and resources however you want. You can also customize the case with different charms that provide useful bonuses. Managing your space and deciding what to carry remains an important part of the game without becoming overly frustrating.

The Merchant is also back and better than ever. You can buy and upgrade weapons, sell treasures, and trade special items for useful rewards. The new weapon upgrade system feels very satisfying, and there are plenty of weapons to experiment with.

Exploration has also been improved significantly. The game is still mostly linear, but there are now many more optional areas, hidden treasures, puzzles, and side objectives to discover. The new side quests give you additional reasons to explore the environments, revisit areas, and discover new things as you progress instead of simply following the main path.

The enemies are excellent and much more threatening than in the original. The Ganados are more aggressive, fast, and intelligent, and their animations and reactions make them feel much more alive. The Plagas are still terrifying, and the redesigned special enemies are fantastic. Some encounters require specific weapons or strategies, forcing you to adapt instead of relying on a single weapon for everything.

The story is still simple but much better presented. Leon's mission to rescue Ashley remains the core of the adventure, but the remake gives the characters much more development and personality. Leon feels less like a walking action-movie one-liner machine, and Ashley in particular is much more enjoyable as a character. Luis receives significantly more development, and several characters get more believable motivations and interactions. The story still has plenty of ridiculous moments, but they fit much better into the overall experience.

The extra content is also great. The Mercenaries mode is a fantastic addition for replayability, and Separate Ways gives Ada her own campaign with additional story, locations, and gameplay. There are also plenty of unlockables and challenges that give you reasons to replay the game and experiment with different weapons and playstyles.

In short, it's a fantastic remake and one of the best Resident Evil games. It takes an already excellent game and improves the graphics, combat, exploration, characters, and overall presentation while still preserving what made the original so memorable. If you loved Resident Evil 4 (2005), this is absolutely worth playing, and if you've never played the original, this is probably the best way to experience the game. 100% recommended.

It feels pretty redundant to say that the original Resident Evil 4 is one of the most beloved video games of all time. With its effective horror, great action, stellar atmosphere, and plethora of goofy moments, it's not hard to see why it was, and still is, such a cultural phenomenon. It's such a monolithic moment in Capcom's catalog that, for the longest time, most would tell you that a remake for it would be unnecessary. Why remake something that was essentially perfect?  Thankfully, against all odds, this remake is amazing.

The gameplay of the remake, while keeping some mechanics unique to OG RE4, manages to feel completely different and more fluid. The added knife parrying mechanic is a godsend that adds complexity to the combat that was hardly seen by the knife of the original. With the addition of this mechanic, they took out cutscene-based quick-time events, which is a change I am absolutely thankful for.  I think the change further solidifies the remake as its own unique entry in the RE series, that's the impression I got throughout this remake; it's not trying to replace the original, it's trying to pay homage and give its own take on it. The added parry, in my opinion, gives way to significant improvements in your encounters with Krauser, as his quick-time event sequences are replaced with tense knife fights that test what you've learned. They've also removed the red dot sight that used to be a default feature for every weapon; only a select few guns get access to it in this remake. This change adds a little more difficulty to your aiming, but the learning curve is shallow enough to where it was never frustrating to get used to, and it was very satisfying mastering the game's gunplay. I absolutely adore the voice acting (yes, even Ada's). The tough and gruff voice of Leon in this remake is absolutely amazing and does so much to show the player how the events of Raccoon City in RE2 and the training Leon went through changed him as a person.

There are plenty of things the remake keeps that are from the original and it all feels incredibly tasteful. For one, the cheesy one-liners and dialogue are still here. The merchant is back and is still a joy to be in the presence of, with his funky Aussie/cockney accent. Thankfully, they kept the different difficulties to choose from and even made alterations to professional to make it even more extreme. After you complete the game you’re given weapons and costumes as rewards just like the original, and the added ranking system incentivises replaying the game to earn more goodies. The inventory system is fully intact from the original and is still very comfy and satisfying to organise, and they even added a button to auto-sort your items; a nice quality-of-life feature. There are very small things that they kept in that add so much to the experience as well, like the sound of the regenerator’s breathing and the inclusion of the strange moving bag room from the original. These are the kinda nuances in the remake that show that it was clearly made by people who have an immense love and understanding of what makes RE4 such a great game. It would’ve been incredibly easy for them to replace the regenerator’s breathing with some stock monster sounds and give the game’s sound direction the Demon’s Souls remake treatment, but instead they had the forethought to keep these sounds to give the game that authentic RE4 feel with a twist.

There is still so much more to appreciate about this remake that I could go into, but I don’t think I should spoil everything for you guys. If you're a fan of the action-horror genre, you need to play this now. It’s a remake made by fans for fans and newcomers, and you can feel the deep appreciation for the series in every detail of this entry. It’s such a joy to have two masterful RE4s now.

I'll disclaimer this by saying I played through it on hardcore difficulty - but that was the recommended difficulty for someone who'd played the old version according to the game.

Lot of stuff to like about the game.  Unfortunately, much more to dislike.

The new animations are great.  Lots of small details, like Leon checking the chamber or changing his arm position when enemies are extremely close.

The new animations are also terrible.  When coupled with a lack of i-frames when taking damage, you can very easily get combo'd and overwhelmed when an enemy decides to play the "axe gets stuck in your shoulder" animation instead of the regular hit.

The gun changes are great.  Lots of rebalancing across the board to make your choice less binary and more of a playstyle decision.

The gun changes are also terrible.  Forced deviation for a lot of weapons makes them a chore to use.  I didn't realize how critical the pistol laser was until I tried to use the Red 9 with its half-second aim bloom every time you point it at an enemy.  The Handcannon might as well not be in the game.  Even with a stock, the TMP is terrible because the first shot makes it max out deviation.

The knife changes are great.  The parry system makes fights more dynamic and forces you to pay attention to your knife, another limited resource.

The knife changes are also terrible.  What seems like an interesting resource management decision is quickly disillusioned when you realize that the choice is generally "spend 5% knife durability for an instant kill, or spend 30% of your ammo putting down an enemy that randomly decided to change into a tougher enemy".

The movement changes are great.  It feels better than ever to move around and shoot in the game, very responsive controls.

The movement changes are also terrible.  Because you have the ability to slowly walk while aiming, the answer to keeping fights challenging seems to be "just spawn dozens more enemies every fight and turn nearly every boss into a minion boss", which just introduces tons of random, frustrating deaths.  I believe this change was also due to them adding a checkpoint system to lower the loss of progress when you die, which I'd gladly give up in favor of fewer clouds of enemies.

The voice acting changes are great.  Leon, Luis, Salazar, and Ashley really emote well in cutscenes and give off pretty believable performances.

The voice acting changes are also terrible.  Ashley's terror screams in combat are utterly ear piercing and made me want to turn off voice volume whenever she was with me.  Ada's voice actor sounds like a young Roseanne.  I have no clue who voiced her, but they gave a really lifeless performance and the voice was such a mismatch from the appearance of the character that she could've doubled as a radio show host.  The enemy chatter randomizer seems to really favor about 2 lines, especially "AHI ESTA".  I heard that so many times that it lost all meaning.

The story and level changes are generally not great.  It seems like they truncated a lot of the village and castle to extend the time you spend on the island by a lot.  The game really started to drag toward the end, and a lot of the goofy, fun stuff was taken out in favor of...I don't know...more regenerators?  Another mass of dudes arena fight with the wrecking ball?  A longer section with the helicopter at the end?  I'm not sure, exactly.  The island is about as unmemorable as it was in the old game, it just felt like it was 10 times longer.

The crafting, case modification, and spinel systems do little other than add busy work to the game.  I wish I could like them more, but they really don't do much.  The spinels in particular are really egregious because they require you to go back and do chores to get them.  Walking halfway back through the map to spend resources fighting a powered up basic enemy to get a resource that you generally just end up turning into money anyway is just busywork.  I'd rather just go back to pixel hunting for shiny stuff to shoot out of the roof of a cave, honestly.  Crafting is little more than a way to compensate for the less generous random ammo drops, rarely did I ever use it to make a grenade or anything besides a box of shotgun rounds.  The case modification system just sucks.  It really just sucks.  I enjoyed getting bonus models from the old game through the shooting gallery, but the randomized gacha balls are annoying to get charms.  The charms themselves are annoying to deal with, as if you want to maximize your shop efficiency you have to go back and forth between the merchant and the typewriter to swap them out based on what you're trying to buy and sell.  The shop discount ones should just be activated by default.  Most of the others just give you a random chance at crafting more ammo or let you get more health back. 
 Basically just a way to help compensate for bad RNG drops if you get a box full of green herbs and don't want to waste them crafting triple greens.

All in all what the remake does is add a lot of tedium and frustrating randomness to what used to be a pretty well paced game.  When I think back on RE4, I'm still going to be thinking of the old game.  This one holds no staying power for me.  I didn't even bother going for a professional playthrough or getting all the weapon unlocks.  I just don't care to do it again.

Mercenaries mode is still fun.  If you get it on an extremely steep sale, like 80% off, it might be worth it just to play that mode.  Otherwise I'd say just save your money.

The problem with this is that the amorphous "realistic" quality to this game that many people have used as an excuse for an overall downgrades in numerous areas, just makes the game incredibly generic and something that will fade out within a year, if not less, as opposed to RE4 which remained a classic for nearly 2 decades now.

You have to look nowhere further than the gameplay changes. The parry and "aim-while-walking" additions are so good they almost make up for the fact that they are merely "band-aid" solutions to the fact that Leon controls much less precisely than the original, requiring crutches to blush over these flaws. You could, like some reviewers, claim that this movement is much more "realistic" since Leon's momentum now carries forward. It would do, unfortunately, little to make up for the fact that Leon just feels more frustrating and irresponsive to play now.

Remember how the fans of the OG would affectionately call it a "product of it's time"? Despite the fact it endured so long? Well, that would be a much more fitting label for RE4R, which will probably be dusted and forgotten by the next RE title, if not already by next year.

Salazar, a very memorable character from the original, which was created with a tinge of self-aware irony to be a stupid, midget, napoleon hat wearing idiot, is now played entirely straight and looks bland enough to seem ripped entirely out of RE: Village slop, along with all of the prominent Salazar cutscenes AND conversations being entirely removed from the game.

Saddler has also been significantly dumbed down with the lack of interactions throughout the game, to the point he is physically absent until the very end of the game. Oh, and he also sounds like a literal nerd DM'ing a horror-themed D&D dungeon. We're talking about the main antagonist.

I originally wrote that Krauser was the only better developed villain, but having replayed the original, I no longer believe this. The original Krauser feels like a much better realized villain. He treated you as an equal, called you "Comrade", asked you why you fought, tried to understand you. And the VA behind him fit the character much better. "New" Krauser sounds like a generic sly, power-hungry villain. This is despite the fact that there is now so much transmedia lore to pull from for Krauser, created in the following years after RE4.

Since we're on the topic of cutscenes, let me preface by saying I watch nearly no movies. I'm not at all a movie buff or snub critic. But it is APPARENT that all of the cinematics in this game are done dirty by the lack of interesting angles or any cinematography whatsoever, with none of the sound cues the OG's cutscenes had to keep things entertaining, either. I had noticed this already just by the Bingo line in the Demo, but it became increasingly clear there was no effort behind these cinematics.

This is, by the way, not even the worst of it; we have worse cutscenes, yes, but even more aggregious is that some important cutscenes were cut entirely from the game. Cutscenes that COULD have made the difference in this remake. That COULD have made Salazar anything other than a b-actor who didn't make the cut for Village. Both Salazar and Saddler have at least 5-10m worth of cutscenes cut out of the game EACH.

The graphics, relentlessly chasing a dark and gritty aesthetic, have managed to create areas even worse-looking than those present in a game from 2005. Look no further than the castle area with the pools of "black water" that looked imposing and unique in the original, turned into just some dark space you can barely tell apart the finer details of, in a futile attempt to make what is effectively an action sequence into a "scary spooky area". 

Of course, this affected the characters too. Whereas RE4 reigned supreme in being a self-aware action shlock, RE4R is trying to play entirely ridiculous concepts straight. This means that Leon is no longer the dashing quippy hero of the original, but more like a war veteran suffering from PTSD with SOME quippy lines. There is very little sprinkled of the original's lightheartedness, and what little there is, is just barely enough not to make current Leon edgy as hell. It's a shame, because we've had so many examples of quippy heroes done awfully in recent games, and RE4 Leon is the trope done right, carrying just the right amount of self-awareness. 

It is needless to say, then, that RE4R Leon is much less memorable and holds little of the charm of the original. The VA work for him is solid, but the character does not have it's original charm. In RE4R there is no equivalent to "no thanks, bro" or "you're small time, Saddler", so I don't foresee anyone quoting Leon lines in general, imagine two whole decades from now.

And while Leon, Luis and Ashley's voicework is solid, the remaining VA's all lose out to it's OG counterparts despite how far the game's industry has come in terms of professional voice acting. Every time Ada speaks, I feel like I'm watching porn. Salazar and Saddler are genuine catastrophes. Wesker's identity is almost 90% defined by the manneurisms D.C Douglas added to the role, and boy is he a disappointment. 

Even the Ganados, Garradores, and whatever other enemies have much less memorable sound cues and "tells", despite the fact that the quality of the audio is technologically superior. This drives home the fact that while RE4R has better tech than the OG, it lacks human technique, experience and sensible design, given how important the "tells" were to telling at a glance what you were dealing with. 

Worse still, they extended the gameplay during the Village and Castle sections of the game, which, while by itself positive, was ruined by the fact that we traded so many sections entirely cut out of the game for more of the same areas just extended by a bit. It feels cheap, like they were strapped for resources and had to extend their existing assets rather than create the one's missing (which is by now part and parcel of the RE remake game design). We have bosses entirely missing from the game, iconic scenarios just poofed out of it.

Let me name a FEW missing locations from Leon's campaign: the underground cave area was missing several areas, the U-3 boss fight is entirely gone, the lava room in the Castle, several open areas within the Castle courtyards, and the entire truck section.

This game IS one of the better things that's put out there these days, but it's nowhere near the original. If anything, it just showcases the franchise lost the plot entirely. A friend of mine once said that "RE is more about B-horror James Cameron explosion bullshit than Romero-style horror", and he was absolutely right.

But now, they try to make RE games these "seriously serious horror plots" with "totally flawed humans", and play characters which are meant to be campy, nearly entirely straight. And they make this change, no less, to the game that played it's campy charm the best in the entire franchise, bringing to the table no particular innovations to a game that revolutionized the entire action-genre. 

The fact that this game is considered anything better than a 7/10, goes to show more about the state of the industry than any quality this game holds by itself. It's worse than RE4, by a wide margin, and being even somewhat relative to it is enough to be called a "masterpiece".

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
The Remake of Resident Evil 4 is not the masterpiece that everyone thinks it is. After 18 years, we got the Remake of one of the most beloved games ever, yet this reimagined version leaves something to be desired regarding the quality control department. Join me in tackling the good and the bad of the modern version of this title. 

[h1] Control and Gameplay [/h1]
Resident Evil 4 Remake has the same problems that The Evil Within had back in the day: it was poorly tested. Dying in the Remake is good, literally. For this example, let's grab the Salazar as a special guest. He is a fascinating boss fight; you have to dodge his attacks while striking when he is exposed! He moves fast and can deal massive damage, so you must get in the mindset and be cold-blooded to win.

Sadly we die, but is this a bad thing? We return to the beginning of the fight with all our munition and items. There is no fear; I follow tracks A, B, and C and finish him in 2 minutes. My reward for losing that boss fight is ending in a good position with extra ammo. Do you think this is a good design? Some areas can be the hardest because of one enemy with Molotovs, but I can snipe him, and then it's the most straightforward battle. The desgarrador is easy to kill, while surviving with Luis in the village is insanely hard. The balancing of the game seems lazy. The Remake is excellent, but some parts are incredibly easy, and others are...quite the struggle.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2962035954

I played the game in Standard difficulty. The game also suffers from rushing since, at times, the title can be inconsistent in giving items to the player. The Deluxe Edition and Pre-Order bonuses allow one to get ammo drops more accessible and get extra money, making them valuable resources for the campaign. Still, it gives a sense that Capcom is saying, "Hey, maybe you want to buy all the extras?" You can also buy tickets to upgrade weapons for free for real money, so it begs the question: Did Capcom make the game's balance poor on purpose? 

[h1] Graphics[/h1]
The game was tested with an RTX 2060, 36 GB of ram, Intel Core i7-11700K - Core i7 11th Gen Rocket Lake 8-Core 3.6 GHz LGA 1200.

The title looks great, but sadly, the island isn't the best location to show the beautiful graphics. Some parts are generic, while others are a bit simple. Unto more positive notes, the lighting effects are fantastic while the show of explosions and bullets is very crips on the screen. The models are incredible; Leon, Ashley, and the rest of the cast look their best. 

To run the game, you will need at least mid-range specs similar to mine or compromise in settings/resolution; I got half the graphics in medium and half in high and a stable 72 FPS. There was only one hard crash during my experience with the game that made me close it; apart from that, it was a smooth adventure overall. 

[h1] Sound[/h1]
The sounds are realistic, and the sources come from the direction in-game. Everyone who played the original can enjoy the classic "Behind you, imbecile" taunt from foes striking from the blindspot. The voice actors nailed the roles, and there is a lot of ambiance in the noises you can hear during the darkest sections of the game (mind you, the regenerators are as spooky as they were in 2005, if not more!)

[h1] Story and Characters [/h1]
The story follows Leon S. Kennedy. After surviving the events of Resident Evil 2 Remake, he is now a full-fledged special agent and must rescue the president's daughter Ashley Graham. It is an action/thriller story with many exciting moments and interesting characters. Some areas last a lot, so the pacing can be slow, but overall everything flows adequately, a remarkable tale for newcomers and a nostalgic trip remodeled for veterans!

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2962036468

Ashley is as annoying as she was back in 2005, and sometimes your "companions" are more of a curse than a blessing, as even Luis forgets to shoot enemies and stands in your way. Thankfully there is no need to be always accompanied on the long journey. Krauser is the best in visuals and making a presentation in his spectacular boss fights! He is fast and cocky in how he treats Leon as a rookie who knows no better than to try to be the good guy in the situation. Salazar also is visually detailed and provides a menacing and macabre atmosphere when appearing on screen. 

[h1] Replayability [/h1]
Don't let the 8 hours speedrun achievement fool you. RE4R is a long game taking around 14-17 hours to beat, and it took me 13 hours to see the credits roll aiming for the speedrun. After clearing the game, there is a huge invitation to replay in more severe difficulties or for the speedrun. If none of those fancy you, there is also the free Mercenaries mode and future DLC that will be Separate Ways, adding more story and focusing on Ada.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2962036184

[h1] Conclusion[/h1]
Resident Evil 4 Remake is a fantastic game; there is no denying that. However, during my experience, I felt I died in unfair situations quite a bit, leaving me with a bittersweet aftertaste. A great game to get at full total price, RE4R brings a masterpiece to the modern era and is an excellent opportunity to explore one of the best games ever made. It doesn't quite hold to the original and suffers from problems that RE3R suffers, but it is good to see Capcom doing better in its games.

I don't like remakes. 

Maybe you'll "recapture the magic" or whatever, but you'll probably just ruin something great for future generations. 

Well, I was wrong. This time. 

RE4 Remake takes the 2004 original and translates it perfectly into a shooter from 2023. 

Does it reinvent the genre, the way the original did? No. 

But it was never going to do that. It isn't *trying* to do that. 

Leon is a different guy in the remake. Still sexy, still funny, but younger and less of a smirking badass. Something lost, something gained; he's more believable, and it's easier to imagine him never getting over his experiences with Ada. 

Every location and set piece from the original is here, except U-3, which sucked anyway, and you know it. 

Some parts, like the shooting gallery, are significantly improved. Other things, like hiding ulockables behind speedruns -- "remember, don't play the game, just run past it" I had to keep reminding myself -- are worse. 

There's a tendency to suggest that the art is muted and "soulless" in the remake, but it's not. Watch all the comparisons you want, but when you're playing the actual game, the art fits the atmosphere and that atmosphere is immersive and, unlike the original, occasionally stressful and scary. 

Also, Ashley is so much better in the remake I feel like Capcom deserves a reward of some kind. A medal. Maybe some kind of plaque. "Fixed Ashely," it would say. 

New Ashley is neither a helpless damsel nor a shrewish jerk, and when Leon bends to help her up over a ledge or catches her after a big jump, you really care about her. When she fights to save you and screams in terror after you take a big hit, you really feel like she cares about you. 

Really, a medal. A statuette, maybe, like at the Oscars. 

RE4R is harder than the original. The two difficulties: "normal" and "professional" are traded for four very different experiences: Easy, Normal, Hardcore, and Professional. All the best stuff requires doing Professional, and doing it quickly. 

And professional sucks. 

I mean, no, it's great I guess, but it's *hard*. And if, like me, you suck at video games, you'll probably end up playing parts of the game over and over again. 

I've put over 200 hours into a game you can *technically* beat in 4. Do the math. 

Anyway, it's doable, but it's a huge jump in difficulty over the original. 

Finally, do yourself a favor and download two mods from Nexus. One that mutes Leon's cough -- he makes this little noise when he aims, over and over again, it's baffling and irritating -- and another that cuts Ashley's sex noises. What sex noises, you ask? Well, when she runs, she makes endless little hentai sounds that are fun for about 2 minutes, but after that are just distracting. Muting these noises will *dramatically* improve your gameplay experience, and won't take away from the actual game. I promise. 

Anyway, go ahead and drop the money on this one, if you liked the original. All the jokes and stuff are in here. You won't be disappointed.
